title: Editorial: The audit report into the ANU's catastrophic restructure is a bracing document
text:
Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

The audit report confirms what has long been obvious: the Australian National University’s catastrophic restructure was neither necessary nor prudent. It was decided on by a council with limited insight and only arbitrary financial details. When it was clear it was failing, no changes were made.

According to the auditor-general, when the university council endorsed the scheme it had no clear evidence that $250 million in annual savings were “needed, achievable, urgently required, or likely to have the intended impact”.

It did so “without a clear understanding of the problem, the options available, implementation risks, or the expected impact of the program on the university’s purpose, financial sustainability, and people”.

The university spent $35.9 million attempting to implement the restructure. It abandoned it before its projected savings were met.

Throughout its decision-making, council was not provided with detailed financial reporting. There was no real detail about the university’s financial trajectory and no attempt to explain the basis for forecasts.

The consultancy group Nous was initially paid $1.2 million for “strategic change support”. It was contracted for further work valued at up to $2 million, although the audit office saw no invoices for this work.

“A more robust decision-making process by Council should have considered additional information, options, and perspectives, to achieve sustainable structural improvement to the ANU budget,” the auditor-general wrote. “As of January 2026, people risks and revenue risks remain.”

The council accepts the findings but disputes the characterisation. “The program was developed in a dynamic environment, with analysis, options, risks and impacts refined iteratively through engagement between the executive and Council, and subject to ongoing governance and oversight following approval.”

The story of the ANU is the story of Australia’s university sector, captured by spivs and corporate dislocation. Successive governments forced universities to rely on international students and then abandoned them when those students disappeared.

Academics have been forced into sessional work and teaching has become increasingly remote. Campus life has suffered, as has research. Meanwhile, university councils have been overrun by businesspeople and consultants. Money is everywhere except where it should be.

There is one bright moment in the sorry debacle of Renew ANU. The academic deans fought back. They organised. The fool restructure was halted and more sensitive reforms will replace it. The vice-chancellor is gone and the chancellor has followed her.

The audit report is a bracing document. Like all reports that tell the truth, it has been described as scathing. Hopefully its 70-odd pages will be read across university councils. Hopefully it will be a reminder to the suits who sit on them that what they are running is more precious and more fragile than a simple business. It is the intellectual life of the country.
